newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Ortiz shrugs off Q1 corporate results.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Ortiz shrugs off Q1 corporate results.

text.p: Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz on Tuesday said first quarter corporate results may have been weaker than expected but he remained confident about the overall performance of the economy and expected purchasing power to pick up in the second half.

"We can have a quarter where the company results may be lightly below expectations and the general results of the economy may be in line with expectations or perhaps a bit better. We think that economic activity is in line," he told reporters after a joint news conference with U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.

Ortiz said the first quarter earnings were affected by a number of factors, including low raw material prices, "but company results are not necessarily correlated with the results of the productive process in the same period."

Ortiz has predicted that Q1 economic growth will be between five and six percent, based on what he sees as strong industrial production data, healthy sales of gasoline and diesel and robust value added tax and income tax receipts.

Analysts have said Q1 quarterly results fell short of expectations in nearly every sector, pouring cold water on hopes the Mexican economy was staging a strong comeback from its 1994-5 economic crisis.

One of the biggest drawbacks on growth has been lingering weakness in consumer demand, but Ortiz predicted there would be a bounce in purchasing power in the second half of this year, partly because of an improving job market.

"What we're seeing is that employment is coming on well and that contract negotiations that have been underway are contemplating salary hikes above expected inflation -- not necessarily above past inflation, but above expected inflation."
He noted that Mexicans are still in debt in general, and that improving purchasing power will not immediately translate into higher consumer spending because those debts still have to be repaid.
"It's going to be a gradual process, but the important thing is that salary deterioration has stopped and we are beginning to see a recovery of earnings," Ortiz said.
